body:
Alright, I'll split this PR into 2 parts. 

About:
> the second (https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/commit/7e719c9e4ba697e064a7fbf21288cdf543e94a33) seems somewhat invasive and also really specific, to the point that I don't think we should land it. 

I mean people prefer using `Option::unwrap_or` over manually matching seem to be benefit from this suggestion.

> Putting a new suggestion right into the middle of the argument checking logic seems like the wrong thing to do IMO

I don't understand what it means. That change add a new suggestion in `fn report_arg_errors` 
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/bcf1f6db4594ae6132378b179a30cdb3599a863d/compiler/rustc_hir_typeck/src/fn_ctxt/checks.rs#L482
and it is laid after `suggest_ptr_null_mut`, which is also a suggestion:
https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/bcf1f6db4594ae6132378b179a30cdb3599a863d/compiler/rustc_hir_typeck/src/fn_ctxt/checks.rs#L944-L949

@rustbot ready
r? compiler-errors

body: I'm a bit confused by the original issue. It used `x test A B` as an example, but most tests should be handled by [this](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/73028fe48320766d5dd931394c2d7b17bed14646/src/bootstrap/src/core/builder.rs#L464), and thus they should already be handled in the original order. Is there an example of a different command where order is important, but which is not handled by the suite logic?
author: Kobzol

body:
> It used x test A B as an example, but most tests should be handled by [this](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/73028fe48320766d5dd931394c2d7b17bed14646/src/bootstrap/src/core/builder.rs#L464), and thus they should already be handled in the original order.

That's not quite right. The logic below handles the step executions most of the time. The one you linked is supposed to handle specific test paths (like `tests/something/test.rs`).

To debug the ordering, you can run this command:

`x test clippy miri bootstrap rustdoc sysroot --dry-run | grep Testing`

and compare the CLI order to the executed steps.

body:
> @tgross35 I have updated the pull request. Now it breaks external libraries like ide-assist. It should be fixed by [Supertrait item shadowing](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3624?w=1). Is there a way to activate both features and see if everything works as intended?

That PR is a draft so it is not ready yet. That feature will fix the conflicts with `itertools` on _stable_ features, there shouldn't be any conflict for unstable features. But it will raise the `unstable_name_collisions`, as seen in the RA build failures (you can fix these either by using the suggested fully qualified syntax, or with `#[allow(unstable_name_collisions)]`).

You can try it locally to see the interactions. After you build you can do `rustup toolchain link stage1 ...` (see https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/building/quickstart.html), and then `cargo +stage1 ...` in a test crate to use it.

author: GuillaumeGomez

body: You will have to make cg_gcc's build system respect `--out-dir` for the sysroot build directory too. But even aside from that, bootstrap sets a fair amount of rustflags and a rustc wrapper which interferes with building the standard library. This is the reason why for cg_clif I chose to test using the sysroot built by cg_llvm rather than building the standard library using cg_clif. What you can do however is having a ci job which only enables the gcc backend. Then the standard library will be built using cg_gcc.

body:
I've fixed the imports.

Ideally we'd enforce via lint at least that `inherent::*` is preferred over manually importing traits from that module, since almost certainly never want to import specific trait names from there, but that seems like a lot of effort. Seems easy to mess up with rust-analyzer's auto-imports unfortunately :(

Would prefer if we try to keep these imports clean in general 🤔 I've tried very hard to clean them up in the process of uplifting and I think it does a lot to help the code maintainability.

body: Hello, @SamuelMarks. This is not an oversight, it was quite intentional. See [this comment from ExitCode's stabilization](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/93840#issuecomment-1045160700) and [this one in a similar PR](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/125182#issuecomment-2115755918).
author: workingjubilee
workingjubilee

body:
In that case, what standard type should I use to percolate exit codes all the way up to `fn main`?

(and yes, I already `impl std::ops::FromResidual<Result<std::convert::Infallible, MyError>>
    for SuccessOrMyError<std::process::ExitCode>` and `impl<T> std::process::Termination for SuccessOrMyError<T> {` and that calls `impl std::process::Termination for MyError {`)

Would a [`code`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/process/struct.ExitStatus.html#method.code) [hyperlink is to `ExitStatus`] implementation have a PR accepted?
author: SamuelMarks

body:
> In that case, what standard type should I use to percolate exit codes all the way up to fn main?

Could you describe this motivation a little more clearly? It sounds like you have synthesized a few different ExitCodes, either via the SUCCESS or FAILURE constants, or via the `From<u8>`, and when you finish running this process, you have a few different ExitCodes generated elsewher, and you want to pick which one to return using some kind of comparator?
author: workingjubilee

body: or... wait, you just want to run tests? were the tests asserting on ExitStatus?
author: workingjubilee

body:
@workingjubilee More than just run tests, this large Rust project I forked is oriented towards CLI-only usage. I'm going through it and replacing all `panic`s and other termination points with `Result` or `Either` types, percolating up `ExitCode`s all the way up until `fn main`.

_But_, in tests I need to compare that the right `ExitCode` is found, and perhaps in non `SUCCESS` cases from `main`—or a function in the backtrace—it will be used to retry something a certain number of times, and if `SUCCESS` is not reached, then return whatever the last `ExitCode` was and terminate the process.
author: SamuelMarks

body:
Oh okay, so a hypothetical most-minimal addition would be that you want `ExitCode::is_success` to exist?

I'm not the final word on whether this API change should be accepted, I'm just trying to note things that are going to be asked about at some point or another and trying to discern the motivation. A change that answers a specific motivation is often more persuasive than one that has an unclear motivation.

And for `is_success`, ["Should we add `is_success` to ExitCode?"](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/48711#issue-302050436) is even listed as an unresolved question in the original tracking issue. While it seems PartialEq was explicitly rejected, [`is_success` was seemingly shelved for later consideration](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/48711#issuecomment-1548148133). And you are not the only one who wants such a function, for basically the same reasons it seems: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/113081

libs-api could choose to reconsider the earlier decision about PartialEq, or might prefer to just add a function returning a bool. An ExitCode _is_ deliberately vague, but "success or not?" seems like a reasonable question to answer.
author: workingjubilee

body:
We discussed this in today's @rust-lang/libs-api meeting.

For forwards compatibility with potentially weird future targets, we'd like to initially just support `PartialEq`.

Also, could you please update this PR to update the documentation as well? Right now, the documentation says "and intentionally does not provide accessors like `PartialEq`, `Eq`, or `Hash`.". This clause should be deleted, and replaced by something like "For forwards compatibility with potentially unusual targets, this type currently does not provide `Eq`, `Hash`, or access to the raw value. This type does provide `PartialEq` for comparison, but note that there may potentially be multiple failure codes, some of which will *not* compare equal to `ExitCode::FAILURE`."

author: rustbot

body: We recreate the `InterpCtxt` on every constant, so this does not do any cross-constant caching, which is where it is actually needed I believe. This would need to work similar to how we create only a single alloc id for static items.
author: oli-obk

body:
Oh, I didn't realize `InterpCtxt` isn't shared.

Does it mean I should put the cache in `GlobalCtxt` and use [`TyCtxt::allocate_bytes`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/beta/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/context/struct.TyCtxt.html#method.allocate_bytes) to allocate global memory for these strings?
`AllocId/Pointer` is unique globally and `InterpCtxt` can read global memory so it should work.
author: adwinwhite

body: I think changing `allocate_bytes` to use https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nightly-rustc/rustc_middle/ty/struct.TyCtxt.html#method.reserve_and_set_dedup internally will do exactly what we want, as we already have a cache
author: oli-obk

body:
This approach looks elegant!

The only problem is that [`reserve_and_set_dedup`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nightly-rustc/src/rustc_middle/mir/interpret/mod.rs.html#535) doesn't work with `GlobalAlloc::Memory(..)`.
Should we inline an unrestricted version of `reserve_and_set_dedup` into `allocate_bytes` by hand or just allow `GlobalAlloc::Memory` in `reserve_and_set_dedup`?
author: adwinwhite

body:
> just allow `GlobalAlloc::Memory` in `reserve_and_set_dedup`?

yea, we originally restricted it because we didn't have a use case, so it seems fine to just remove the check and permit it

body:
This PR bumps `invalid_type_param_default` to an FCW that **does** report in deps, and removes the `default_type_parameter_fallback` feature gate which currently exists **solely** to suppress that lint. Given the complicated nature of type parameter fallback, this feature deserves a total redesign and right now represents a (very light, but still worth cleaning up) tech debt burden in the compiler.

Given the feature being an (intended) type system feature, this seems to me a pretty clear types FCP.

There should be no fallout (so ignore the crater run above) since this PR was adjusted **not** to bump the lint to an error but instead just make the FCW report in deps, due to a lot of fallout (namely, lots of transitive dependents of `typemap`).

body: I doubt anyone cares enough to sway this FCP, but [function type parameter defaults act the same as ADT type parameters defaults](https://quinedot.github.io/rust-learning/misc-default-param.html#default-type-parameters-elsewhere) as far as I know.  They're worse off mainly because you can't name function item types.

body:
Thanks for the info @QuineDot, but I don't really think users should really be using of default type params on functions anyways. If this is heavily requested, I think we can add this feature gate back with a proper lang team experiment to investigate supporting default params the *right* way (i.e. in a more ergonomic way).

author: tgross35

body:
Thanks for pointing out `syn`.  In posting the stabilization report and thereby signaling the intention to stabilize, we mean to uncover things like that so that we can work to get them resolved.

More widely, the unfortunate reality is that most nightly-only features like this just don't get a lot of actual testing in nightly.[^1]  So there is often limited testing value in leaving an otherwise-ready feature in nightly for an extended period of time.[^2]

In this case, what's being stabilized are the minimal and well-understood pieces.  As the stabilization report describes, we're lowering this to expose existing type system features in which we have high confidence.[^3]

There are three key reasons to get this out sooner rather than later:

1. It gives people more time to migrate their code ahead of the edition.
2. Independent of the edition, it solves a real problem that users have (overcapturing of lifetimes), and it's worth delivering that value to our users on stable Rust.
3. **It derisks the edition.**

Putting on my edition hat, *number 3* is really key here.  To achieve our goals for the edition, which are:

- Make this edition a success.
- Do so without requiring heroics from anyone.
    - ...or stressing anyone or everyone out.

We need to be (and are) crossing off as many items as possible as soon as possible.  Things always go wrong, and trying to wait until the last minute for anything is a recipe for putting the edition plans at risk or stressing everyone out to try to make a diving save.

This isn't the only item that's going to be like this.  We have other edition items where the feature needs to be stabilized in all editions ahead of the edition.  For those too, we're going to want stabilizations to happen sooner rather than later[^4] even though these features have landed only recently in nightly.

Our *go / no go* date for all items is less than three months out at this moment.  That will go by in a blink.  [The edition is on track](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/127672#issuecomment-2226843609).  But to keep it that way, there just isn't that much time that we can delay.[^5]

[^1]: This is, in a way, a *success*.  We want people to use stable Rust and not come to rely on nightly features.

[^2]: Looking at a calendar, this isn't going to stabilize any sooner than Rust 1.82 which will be released on 2024-10-17.  So even if this stabilization entered FCP today, there's yet some further time for testing and for things like `syn` to potentially make accommodations.  That will be 6 months after the feature landed in nightly.

[^3]: It's not without relevance that we have high confidence in the implementor here too.

[^4]: But no sooner than when it's ready and we have high confidence in it, of course.

[^5]: We need the things that *are* ready to get fully crossed off so we can focus on the things that are not yet.
author: traviscross

body:
As a lang advisor, I want to second @tgross35's point and formally raise a concern. Can some lang member please register this with rfcbot when FCP starts (if this isn't resolved in some way).

To start, let me say that I quite like this feature and where it ended up in terms of how you specify the captured parameters. Overall, having this feature will make the language better.

That being said, I have very strong doubts that we as language developers have properly done our due diligence here to ensure that language *users* understand this feature, how to use it, and that it all-in-all brings *down* the net burden of learning Rust.

One reason for this concern is that `impl Trait` *already* is one of the more confusing parts of the language (in part because of the dichotomy between RPIT and APIT and in part because of it's just a being bit of tricky feature because of captures/lifetimes). I think it's also clear that we're still as language developers figuring out what opaque types *mean* and can do, given both ongoing work like TAITs, but also unanswered questions around higher-ranked lifetimes (which depending what we decide results in different outcomes for things like async closures). So, adding on additional complexity to `impl Trait` being "sure" that we understand how it affects the language for users for be a massive fail for us as language developers (not to mention that "additional complexity" is the largest thing users said they were worried about in the 2023 survery).

Another reason I'm raising this concern is that, especially given the above, in my option this feature has moved very fast through its developmental milestones and we ultimately lack data on how this might or will be used. The reasoning that "we don't expect much nightly usage" is extremely concerning. It is ultimately true, but that doesn't mean that we can't do better. To give some ideas, we could 1) do a thorough analysis of existing code to identify patterns were this needed or how it affects code readability 2) put out calls for testing or surveys of the proposed feature 3) dogfood this more, in the compiler itself for example.

To also add another point to the above: the discussion of this feature since conception has resulted in a *significant* change with the syntax change from `use <..>impl Trait` to `impl Trait + use<..>`. (Which as I have said before I do like,  but is still a significant change.) This to me highlights the complexity in the feature and the need to *properly* understand its effect on language use.

All in all, I think it's pretty clear that the timeline for this is heavily accelerated by the edition. But let me note: there will be more editions. We do not need to, nor should we, rush features through because of some arbitrary constraint of them needing to make it into *this* edition. Ultimately, without the proper work I suggest above, I don't think this feature should make the edition *and that's okay*. And further, doing the things I suggest above is itself a big ask, and I don't think would get done in time for the edition (though, that's not a given).

@traviscross to directly address your "make the edition a success without requiring heroics or stressing anyone and everyone out": not landing this feature will *not* make this is edition unsuccessful, but rushing it definitely does stress people out (if not anybody else (which I doubt), at least very much me).

Our ethos is not to rush features for arbitrary deadlines. In the past, we've done a mixed job at following that with editions. This, in my opinion, is one of the stronger examples of us letting the timeline of the edition dictate when feature development milestones must happen by, rather than them co-occuring naturally and mostly independently.

And finally, I want to point out a large concern from me with the edition as it relates to this as well: we have already pushed the stability of the edition to 2025, in large part (likely, I haven't been a part of those decisions) because features like this could not have been ready in time. To me, this is a large hint that we're trying to do too much. I would *much* prefer a "smaller edition" (if you can say that, it's still 3 years of development work) than trying to fit everything in it for some arbitrary line of "success" at the expense of both a delay *and* rushing features through.
author: jackh726

body:
I'd definitely like to echo some of jack's points here.

Reading through TC's comment I generally get the impression that there "isn't much time" and we "have to stabilize everything ASAP", this really feels to me like the 2024 edition has "gone wrong" somehow. In an ideal world I don't think we should be 6months out from an edition release worrying about landing RFCs and stabilizing features.

In general I am a bit concerned that the "deadline" of the edition acts as an intentional (or unintentional) pressure to rush things in that are not necessarily ready or the best solution. I think regardless of the fact precise captures seems relatively straightforward and I'm in favour of it, the framing here of "we have to get this in quickly for the edition" makes me distinctly uncomfortable.

We have the train release schedule *for a reason* and the fact that things are happening so close to shipping the edition to the point where we're even talking about whether its *possible* to wait a few cycles before stabilization is deeply concerning to me.

I would definitely say that the feeling of there being so many "last minute" RFCs for this edition *is* stressing me out. As a concrete example the fact that Match Ergonomics 2.0 is seemingly still having its design figured out is *so very worrying*. Match ergonomics being probably one of the more controversial features the language has and we're increasing its strength all the while rushing to "get it out the door" for the edition.

I don't know that I really have a good solution here other than "it sure would be nice if we started work on the edition significantly earlier for 2027".

---

Interestingly, I don't think this really has anything to do with the "quality" of the feature- I find the broad strokes of the match ergonomics proposal to be quite compelling. I think never type stuff is super great. I also think precise captures is an incredibly good idea compared to simply shipping the edition captures changes without a way to pare down the captured lifetimes.

Its simply just that the passive pressure (or explicit pressuring in this PR) of the edition deadline makes the whole thing feel significantly scarier than it otherwise would be.
author: BoxyUwU

body:
@jackh726: If you would, it would be helpful if you could describe concretely what you would want to see happen to resolve your concern.  I.e., what's the acceptance criteria for your concern to be resolved?  E.g., is there a specific amount of time you want to see this sit in nightly?  Is there a specific amount of usage you want to see of this in the ecosystem?  Is there a way you would suggest to measure when "we as language developers have properly done our due diligence here to ensure that users understand this feature, how to use it, and that it all-in-all brings down the net burden of learning Rust" (and how do you weigh that against the other reasons to do this)?

With respect to this feature and the edition, not landing this means not landing the Lifetime Capture Rules 2024, which means that the capture rules would work inconsistently between RPIT in bare functions and inherent impls and RPIT in trait impls and in RPITIT[^1] throughout the next edition, as the new rules are already stabilized for the latter (which was done on the expectation of stabilizing these rules across the board in Rust 2024).  It would mean leaving unaddressed for the next edition all of the [problems](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3498-lifetime-capture-rules-2024.md#background) that led us to adopt [RFC 3498](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3498).

It's for these reasons that lang identified this as priority item for Rust 2024.  Not landing this or the other lang priority items, would, in my view, make the edition *less* of a success.

With respect to the edition schedule more broadly -- and I don't want to make this thread about that, so let's please take this aside if we have anything further -- we rescheduled the edition because the other schedule that we inherited wasn't *realistic*.[^2]  None of the lang priority items would have shipped.  Shipping *almost anything at all* in the edition would have required heroics and would have stressed everyone out.  Cutting everything or almost everything would have wasted a ton of work that people had already done, probably burning many of those people out.  **It didn't seem worth doing.**  Taking from the rescheduling the implication that we're trying to do too much is not grounded in the facts of the situation, in my view.

[^1]: ...and in ATPIT and TAIT, when we stabilize those, which we expect to do early in Rust 2024.

[^2]: Mistakes were made.

author: BoxyUwU

body:
# author note read this 😺

Howdy y'all. First of all, thanks for the feedback. *For the record*, I expected this almost certainly to happen, I hope there's no hard feelings mutually on this. Pardon me, I could've probably also made this a zulip thread on T-lang going "are we ready yet?", but also there's always the risk that we *do* that, and people still come out of the woodwork on the stabilization PR, so 🤷 😸.

One problem here is that we don't really have a policy for exposing users to a new nightly feature, teaching them about it, etc. Sometimes this happens after the stabilization PR merges (e.g. on a blog post which happens [*after*](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2023/12/21/async-fn-rpit-in-traits.html)), but this is *especially* uncommon before stabilization, and if it does happen, then it currently happens via osmosis, or for the *largest* features incidentally (e.g. via a blog post that serves an orthogonal purpose).

Many features in Rust sit around unstabilized (but also not gaining much more user exposure at all 😿) for years because they're otherwise blocked on either implementation challenges, or someone hasn't sat down and thought about the feature's consistency as a whole (e.g. associated type bounds), or simply because nobody has written up a stabilization report. The difficulty of developing things in Rust is a natural speed-bump for getting things done, but also that cannot be the only thing that ensures we temper our enthusiasm for stabilizing things we think are ready for prime-time.

So when that doesn't happen (i.e. when developing a feature is straightforward, and it serves a clear purpose in the language, the design isn't particularly ambiguous except for perhaps syntax, etc), such as with this feature, it can feel rushed for two separate but somewhat easy to mix up reasons -- one, is that the stabilization *is* happening quickly, and the second is the feeling that we haven't done our due diligence regarding making sure the feature is ready for stabilization yet. If it were **just** the former, then that's actually a *good* thing IMO, because I think on the contrary the Rust community often perceives that we as compiler developers don't get things done soon enough for what seems like arbitrary process reasons (cue the features that people have been begging about for years -- this is actually one of them, at least at a high level).

BUT regarding that second one which is more important here -- the perception that we haven't done our due diligence making sure the feature is ironed out and ready -- I'll admit that we may be lacking exposure for this feature and haven't made folks as confident as we are regarding whether this is ready 😺 So yeah, as TC said above, it would be very cool to know what people want to see regarding that. Super actionable things like dogfooding in the compiler, making a blog post about it, etc. are all great ideas and I'm interested in doing that very soon.

I do think we really should strike a balance here though, because implementation-wise this feature is pretty simple (in the compiler) and a time-based criteria for waiting for things to be "ready" somewhat discredits that fact, so I'd like to see more *objective*, *tangible* criteria that can be used to gauge a feature's stabilization readiness. I really hope that whatever we learn from this stabilization PR can help us form a larger *roadmap skeleton* for stabilizing features in the future. Developing and *especially* stabilizing shit in Rust is incredibly ad-hoc, and it feels like we're inventing policy as we go *all the time* 😸
author: compiler-errors

body:
I'm going to say one last thing about the edition because I've received evidence some may have taken the wrong idea from one of the messages above about it.

## **The edition is on track.**

On the edition team, we have *no concerns* about how things are going with respect to the edition.  We're crossing off items at the rate we expect.  All items have owners.  Those owners are moving things along, and we have good communication with them and with the relevant teams.  We are confident we're going to succeed in:

- Making this edition a success.
- Doing so without requiring heroics from anyone.
    - ...or stressing anyone or everyone out.

The point above is about what we need to see happen to *keep it on track*.

The plan that's been working has been to push all of the items along as we can to *completion*, and to cross off items that can be made *ready* as soon as possible so we can focus on the remaining items.

What would break this system is to start saying for the items, "oh, we have `M` months left, let's hold off for `M - ε` on this item."  Then 1) we'd end up behind the airplane and 2) a bunch of items and remaining work and *risk* would pile up at the end.  That's what we cannot do.
author: traviscross

body:
I don't necessarily think that moving swiftly is a problem, and, like the others, I think this feature is a step in the right direction. However: I would suggest that if time for natural community engagement is cut short, it needs to be compensated with effort to somehow get that community engaged. This is _especially_ true with things that arguably make the language more complex, [given the general awareness of that area](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2024/02/19/2023-Rust-Annual-Survey-2023-results.html#challenges).

A related concern is that the feature appears reasonable, but I haven't found any real-world use to see how it feels in situ. [It does not appear to be used within the rust-lang org](https://github.com/search?q=org%3Arust-lang+%2F%28%3F-i%29%5Cbuse%3C%5B%5Cw%5Cs%2C%27.+%5D*%3E%2F+lang%3Arust+AND+%28NOT+path%3Atests%29&type=code), [nor in any codebase on GitHub](https://github.com/search?q=lang%3Arust+%2F%28%3F-i%29%5Cbuse%3C%5B%5Cw%5Cs%2C%27.+%5D*%3E%2F+AND+%28NOT+path%3Acompiler%29&type=code&p=1) (currently 191 total hits, all look like false positives). 

Actionable items that I think may improve the situation:

1. A blog post giving the bigger plan of 2024 lifetime captures and its status would be great. Just saying what components are implemented and ready for testing, what is expected to stabilize next or how that will be broken up, what still has work to do, what lints are coming, how to test it, etc. (Totally different feature but [the GATs post did a great job of this](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2021/08/03/GATs-stabilization-push.html)). I think everyone not on the design team was a bit caught off guard by this PR precisely because very few people were aware it was stable enough for experimentation, much less a stabilization candidate.
2. Update some codebase somewhere to make use of this feature, since it is helpful to see how things change. Agreed with the above that updating the compiler makes sense, but that doesn't have to be it.
3. > This isn't the only item that's going to be like this. We have other edition items where the feature needs to be stabilized in all editions ahead of the edition. For those too, we're going to want stabilizations to happen sooner rather than later even though these features have landed only recently in nightly.
  
    If there are more features requiring accelerated timelines, they should probably follow similar guidelines. That is, as soon as they are usable enough, put out a call for testing (probably just a IRLO/URLO announcement works) as part of due diligence.

In general I do think some policy would help here; when https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3668 was posted and FCP proposal started immediately, I considered suggesting that RFCs should get at least two months from their first TWIR post (which still seems entirely reasonable to me). Two months on nightly after implementation also seems reasonable - enough time for people to come back from vacation, learn about it, come across a use case for it, try it out, and provide feedback. I understand that this PR, and any related features coming, will already be an exception.

Again, I feel positive about going forward here - the writeup is great, the new rules make sense, and I like the new syntax a lot more. We just need to make sure the wider Rust community doesn't feel shorted of its chance to provide input because trying to meet a deadline meant that the feedback loop got cut short.
author: tgross35

body:
Thanks @tgross35.  Those are all reasonable points, in my view.  Some further context and thoughts follow.

### Merging a PR to replace `Captures` with `use<..>` in `rustc`

Regarding updating the compiler to use this feature, we had actually done that ahead of writing the RFC, and [in the RFC](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/3617-precise-capturing.md#migration-strategy-for-lifetime-capture-rules-2024), we linked to [that diff](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/efd136e5cd57789834c7555eed36c490b7be6fe7...0d15c5c62d2a6f46269e5812653900e0945738bf?expand=1) as an example of what this looked like "in action".  We didn't merge it at the time only due to the unpleasantness of adding `#![allow(incomplete_features)]` everywhere.  We'll be updating this to the revised syntax and expect to have a PR up soon.  I've already seen a draft of this.

### Education

One main way that people will find out about and be educated about this feature ahead of and after the release of Rust 2024 is in the [edition guide](https://github.com/rust-lang/edition-guide/).  There will be extensive discussion about the changes to the lifetime capture rules, and that discussion will prominently feature the `use<..>` syntax that we're stabilizing here.  One reason we'd prefer this feature stabilized sooner rather than later is so that we can add this documentation in a way that allows readers today to follow along and migrate their code on stable Rust.

### Outreach and communication

Agreed that more outreach is good.

The RFC was itself a kind of outreach, as is this stabilization report, and this also appeared as part of a flagship Rust project goal, but we can always do more.

### Process and policy

Proposals to change processes often come up in issues like this.  There are things we could talk about doing, e.g. extending the FCP window, but it's probably better to discuss those separately.

body:
> is there a specific amount of time you want to see this sit in nightly?

Very concretely, it is *quite unsurprising* to me that no one has used this feature even if they typically use nightly and may have wanted to. This PR moves this feature gate from being tagged as an "incomplete feature" to stable in one go. I think if we expect nightly usage -- whether in rustc or beyond -- it's very reasonable to expect that users won't reach for features we're explicitly telling them not to use. (At least, that's my understanding of what incomplete feature means).

This is even why we didn't yet experience what at least compiler devs thought of seeing it in code, experiencing things like (just as a potential example) derives/macros breaking due to lack of `syn` support, rust-analyzer error'ing out, maybe rustfmt breaking... historically some of these have been treated as "not a blocker" by lang (though I'm not aware of policy/RFC decisions on the general question), but I think having them as inputs is useful.

> We didn't merge it at the time only due to the unpleasantness of adding #![allow(incomplete_features)] everywhere. We'll be updating this to the revised syntax and expect to have a PR up soon. I've already seen a draft of this.

I think it's pretty reasonable that we allow for *some* time to go by in between a feature being "done" and a feature being proposed for stabilization. The more esoteric/niche features get (as we should expect over time) the harder it is to get people to use them on nightly, but *at least* we can try to dog-food them ourselves and as a fallback have a partner user of some kind that has in fact used these in some code base and can report on how that went.

body:
I've read over the thread and before I respond to anything I want to summarize everything I read.

In terms of "things moving too fast", the points raised are

* The `use` syntax has moved quickly from design to stabilization. Most people are not aware that this syntax exists or how it fits into the larger picture. `impl Trait` is already a source of confusion and therefore we want to be sure that this design will make things easier.
* The syntax is not supported in `syn` and therefore by the majority of procedural macros.

In terms of the edition:

* The goal for the edition is to release "on time" and to avoid stressing folks out. Part of how we accomplish that is moving quickly where we can to avoid last-minute surprises.
* However, targeting a deadline can itself cause stress and cause us to make mistakes. Better to move deliberately and let the chips fall where they may in terms of stabilization.

Am I missing something in this summary?
author: nikomatsakis

body:
The following points are, I think, universally agreed upon:

* The feature is well motivated. We want `-> impl Trait` capture behavior to be consistent across all the places it appears (free functions, inherent methods, trait methods, and in desugaring of async functions). Right now the first two do not capture lifetimes by default and that is distinct from the latter two, which capture all parameters.
* The older `-> impl Trait` capture behavior is a common source of confusion for users. The primary mitigation is compiler suggestions to add `+ '_`, but that constraint can be stronger than necessary, leading to hacky workarounds like `Captures<'tcx>` which are even harder for users to understand (and which have gaps of their own).
* There has always been a need to control captures for `-> impl Trait` but we just haven't had a solution historically.

I think everyone agrees that the proposed design is an improvement on the status quo -- and moreover while I'm always open to hear concerns, I think the bar for raising that *kind of* concern is higher at this stage (that's more appropriate early on). However, @jackh726 had some concern that it hadn't baked long enough for us to have a full picture of how well users will understand it, and/or to think of better alternatives. I think part of what leads to this is that we haven't done a good job telling the "whole story" -- i.e., this particular change is just one part of.a larger alignment, as the first bullet point above hints. (I'm sure @jackh726 is aware of that, but I agree that it's not something we've written about on blog posts etc)

Does this all sound correct?
author: nikomatsakis

body:
I quite liked most of @tgross35's [suggestions](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/127672#issuecomment-2226934903). I propose the following steps...

* author a blog post for the Rust blog that explains the planned changes around impl trait capture and puts them in context; this blog post should also highlight the new `use` syntax and explain that it will be stabilized soon (I'd be happy to drive this, but also happy if someone else wants to take the lead)
* plan for a retrospective lang-team design meeting to discuss how we can avoid "surprise stabilizations" like this in the future (and ensure that @tgross35, @jackh726, @BoxyUwU and others are able to attend if they want to!)

Note there is a [pending PR](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/pull/1707) updating syn to use the next syntax already.

@jackh726, what would you think of that?

-------

There are some suggestions from @tgross35's comment that I intentionally did not echo.

> Update some codebase somewhere to make use of this feature, since it is helpful to see how things change. Agreed with the above that updating the compiler makes sense, but that doesn't have to be it.

I think the [update to the compiler](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch) serves this purpose -- search for `use<` and or `-> impl`. One of the interesting things with this change is that, like the code we saw in the wild, **the new default is almost always what you want**. So "updating a codebase" to use the syntax is often more about removing `+ 'a` and `+ '_` than anything else.

(For the most part, the exceptions in the compiler are instances of the [`IndexVec::indices`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/nightly-rustc/rustc_index/struct.IndexVec.html#method.indices) pattern, where a function reads the length `l` from `&self` and returns an iterator from `0..l` but doesn't need to hold a reference to `self`. There are a few other cases, like [this function that only captures a subset of its arguments](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-47cc8e737635ddb570a3cb869d8bf8bad27e06f588f2838ad5d7fe1192bbc35f).)

> In general I do think some policy would help here; when https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3668 was posted and FCP proposal started immediately, I considered suggesting that RFCs should get at least two months from their first TWIR post (which still seems entirely reasonable to me).

While I am not aligned on this specific idea, I agree that it would be good to think about how we can adjust the process in the future -- hence my proposal for a retrospective above. Rather than rather arbitrary time rules, I'd be more inclined to tweak the process to surface discussions more broadly. In the cases where we are "moving quickly" what is actually happening is that there has been extensive discussion but it hasn't been publicly broadcast, which seems to me like the bigger problem. I do hope that project goals can help here.

author: nikomatsakis

body:
If I understand it correctly, this feature is now blocking #120700, isn't it?
In current stable rust, opaque type is the only way to express a compiler generated type (function as a value, closure or async block/functions) or a complex type inferred by value expressions (eg. values returned by chained operators as `impl Iterator` or `impl Future`). A type that contains such types could never be sealed as a field of a user defined type, or be returned by a trait function that returns an associated type.
Thus library authors have no choice but to avoid returning such types as public API (eg. They cannot return an async operator future directly from an async function, but only a handwritten struct that `impl`s `Future`), otherwise, the usage of the returned type are either limited or needing `dyn` runtime dispatching that brings unnecessary performance cost.
This is an obvious cause that blocks rust from being a mature asynchronized programming language.
As a main purpose of edition 2024, I do think it a significant part of the language updates.

body:
@rfcbot reviewed

Thanks for the excellent writeup, @compiler-errors and @traviscross.

I think we have enough data to be confident that taken together, this feature and the 2024 capture rules it enables _lower_ the overall complexity of using `impl Trait` by a significant amount:

> I think the [update to the compiler](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch) serves this purpose -- search for `use<` and or `-> impl`. One of the interesting things with this change is that, like the code we saw in the wild, **the new default is almost always what you want**. So "updating a codebase" to use the syntax is often more about removing `+ 'a` and `+ '_` than anything else.

I don't think we have publicized the data very much. I tend to agree with Niko that we could avoid such concerns in the future by communicating our intentions more broadly. That said, I still feel confident in the solution we landed on.

Now that the tooling support is in, I don't believe we will get much useful information from a blog post encouraging people to manually enable a flag for this specific feature. I think we will need to have users test the migration itself. That should surface cases where a codebase is made significantly more complex or where the migration could be doing a better job.

Unfortunately I don't think we're completely set up for that... we would need to soft-stabilize this in the (unstable) 2024 edition and give people instructions to run the migration on a nightly project. Is that something we can do?

author: compiler-errors

body:
> I think we have enough data to be confident that taken together, this feature and the 2024 capture rules it enables _lower_ the overall complexity of using `impl Trait` by a significant amount:
> 
> > I think the [update to the compiler](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch) serves this purpose -- search for `use<` and or `-> impl`. One of the interesting things with this change is that, like the code we saw in the wild, **the new default is almost always what you want**. So "updating a codebase" to use the syntax is often more about removing `+ 'a` and `+ '_` than anything else.

I still disagree with this heavily. I'm really not sure why the use of `feature(precise_capturing)` hasn't actually *landed* in the compiler? Is it because we know that once we update to edition 2024 things will just get "cleaned up"? I think that's a poor argument - as you can see in the diff together, there are going to be plenty of remaining uses and many are completely different (e.g. ` + 'a` to `+ use<'tcx>`).

Dogfooding in the compiler is not simply creating a diff that people skim and go "okay, that looks decent", it's about *using the feature in a codebase that gets interacted with daily by many people* and thus getting repeated exposure. Better still is to get repeated *use* so that if usability quarks exist, they get tested and *felt* by people and they can then give feedback.

Really digging into the diff to give some concrete feedback (to show that the decision is here not just "always better", but rather an actual choice between two *decent* options). Though again, we can only get so much of a "feel" of a feature by just "reading" code (I think back to the original decision between `use<> impl` vs `impl use<>` and how @nikomatsakis only really thought it was worth switching after *writing* code examples and getting a feel for it):
1) The implicit capturing of `Self` (or is it impl params?) makes the captures lifetimes less clear. [Here ](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-a8e09394c942976c00fe2a7337b3913bfaf663500297c14813e2e893471542c1R186) and in the entire file it's currently very clear that `'hir` is captured in the opaque type. With the proposed diff, it's imo much less clear.
2) There are [two](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-f0adc1cfaa36cfb676163f88bf97fd49e143b4eb7ee29e4415474182d9ee2907R35) [places](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-47b2e30d6069ccad29d0995f42f0f639aa22bd565a00b23d91a158cabbdf5db9R311) we go from nothing to `use<>`; it's really nice to be able to immediately signal that the opaque type is independent of any params.
3) There [are](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-47cc8e737635ddb570a3cb869d8bf8bad27e06f588f2838ad5d7fe1192bbc35fR1730) [several](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-c5ed083d182591b9031bdbef8c7796619a5b29aa9039e9f2d615e06c4bda770cL65) [places](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-cdbe2d711f33fb056074de90d982e2281661289b3de66f0e62494a204bb6fe7dR133) [where](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-2e6738173d7f2bba108e9eea0ddf6f21bf055752800fc2237abf28849007dcceR392) with the diff we have to "correct" the overcaptures and these are generally more clear but also more verbose.
4) I did see [at least one](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-885afd8bd7572095e2347dc7eabce51cde3f47e07841d705770d94e0fccf2479R1008) place where we went from `+ 'a` to `+ use<'tcx>`. Is *needed*, or is this a "fix" for a more-precise capture?
5) I found a [couple](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:precise-capturing-scratch#diff-4864ab6ed9e5cec3c6d0d561211554aafbd0094842869d2a711b5451151bc534R109) cases where we go from `Captures<'tcx>` -> `+ 'tcx`. Is this just an error in the diff, or did we actually need that over `use<'tcx>`?
6) As @compiler-errors points out, in most places that we had a `+ 'a`, we can just drop that altogether with 2024 capturing rules. I will say, that looking through the code with precise capturing only is definitely more verbose overall (which is not necessarily a bad thing), but as I really read the code and try to think about each diff, I really do get a sense of how *different* this feature is to mentally parse. Having the captured params be at the end of the opaque type and a list really does highlight that the captures are really just that internally; and this is really different to how we generally think about types in the other parts of the language with just "outlives" bounds. I'm not saying this is good or bad, but it certainly gives it a different *feel*. Of course, with the 2024 capture change, they don't appear nearly as often and so you don't get that overall sense of feeling as much, but it is still there.

> I don't think we have publicized the data very much. I tend to agree with Niko that we could avoid such concerns in the future by communicating our intentions more broadly. That said, I still feel confident in the solution we landed on.
> 
> Now that the tooling support is in, I don't believe we will get much useful information from a blog post encouraging people to manually enable a flag for this specific feature. I think we will need to have users test the migration itself. That should surface cases where a codebase is made significantly more complex or where the migration could be doing a better job.

I...don't quite know how to split up these paragraphs and jump in to respond. So, a few thoughts:
1) The compiler diff alone doesn't really sway me much. My concern is and really has been that opaque types are difficult to learn and understand for users, and changing the design around them (as much as we do think the changes are a plus) needs to be met with real data on *user* feedback on whether the changes make it easier or more difficult for them to understand and use opaque types. It's very easy to look at a diff and say "yeah, these changes make sense", but that's predicated on the *feature as-is*. So, ultimately, the problem has not been "communicating our intentions", but rather that most, if not nearly all, the input for this feature has come from within the Project and even then mostly limited to lang + adjacent. There still seem to be no actual uses of this feature (including within the compiler), there have been no blog posts about this, and there have been no issues filed about it. I did find one [reddit thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/rust/comments/1c6k65f/heads_up_2024_edition_will_change_impl_trait/) that sort of covers it, but reactions seem mixed and this is pretty limited in reach and interaction.
2) I guess, the more I think about it, the more I feel like a blog post now is "too late". I'd much rather have had more public interaction throughout the entire design process. Putting up a blog post now isn't *wrong*, but I get the feeling the only useful thing we could do now is have a "this is an upcoming feature and how it works" type of post - which we don't really do often, we sort of did for GATs - and monitor for feedback. I really don't expect that feedback to actually change anyone's mind here though. In large part, I think it's because really nobody has a real alternative solution. So even if the feature does turn out to be really confusing to users, we have no other option to say "is this better" and I don't expect suggestions at this point in the process to be taken seriously.
3) Testing the migration is useful, sure. But for it to be any *real* use to this discussion, people need to work with the migrated code, which just won't happen.

body:
> I'm really not sure why the use of feature(precise_capturing) hasn't actually landed in the compiler?

It's because I literally can't upgrade the compiler to use edition 2024 until https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/14283 is landed on beta, since cargo incorrectly errors on deps with optional features.

I could certainly prepare a PR using `use<>` on edition 2021, but I think as others have said before, the real benefit of this syntax is that most of the time users will be *removing* bounds when paired with the edition 2024 lifetime rules. The only alternative is to add `#![feature(lifetime_capture_rules_2024)]` to every crate in the compiler, which seems unnecessary. If you're willing to review it, I could put up such a PR, though.

> Really digging into the diff to give some concrete feedback [...]

I regret that @nikomatsakis shared that branch that was NOT prepared to land in its current shape, and I want to make it extremely clear that I prepared it **for myself** to gauge the general impact of this feature on a production codebase, and I kinda feel bad that as a result, the work I did there has been put under such a critical microscope, lol. But whatever, that's already been done.

> I will say, that looking through the code with precise capturing only is definitely more verbose overall (which is not necessarily a bad thing) [...]

Right, so, I think this is definitely the wrong way of thinking of it. I think it's much easier to look at the end result -- the way I staged it was mostly to demonstrate how things end up being simpler in edition 2024. I think you mentioned that, though, but I did want to point it out again, explicitly.

Here's a more accurate representation of the migitations that are necessary to make the compiler compile after applying edition 2024: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/compare/master...compiler-errors:rust:ed-2024-fallout?expand=1 -- this PR opts to *overcapture* in some situations where it's not harmful, which I think is the right choice, but obviously something that we cannot do in a migration lint that obviously lacks the context of the whole program.

I expect the edition 2024 guide chapter to mention that users should gauge whether the automatically-inserted `+ use<..>` bound is necessary in practice, and remove it if it is not. I will also work on making the migration lint more accurate, since I don't believe it needs to fire when the overcaptured lifetime params, for example, outlive a lifetime parameter that is already captured by the opaque[^except].

[^except]: Except for what I expect to be an rare case of relating opaques that have different uncaptured lifetimes or something like that.

> Having the captured params be at the end of the opaque type and a list really does highlight that the captures are really just that internally; and this is really different to how we generally think about types in the other parts of the language with just "outlives" bounds.

Well, due to #116733, whether to use `use<>` over `+ 'static` (or `+ use<'a>` over `+ 'a`) in *many* cases is now matter of taste. However, given that change was incomplete due to unsoundnesses around send bounds and uncaptured lifetime params, the fact that an opaque captures lifetimes versus doesn't capture them is still very observable (even with GATs!), so I don't see us getting around that fact any time soon, though.

body:
> I could certainly prepare a PR using `use<>` on edition 2021, but I think as others have said before, the real benefit of this syntax is that most of the time users will be _removing_ bounds when paired with the edition 2024 lifetime rules. The only alternative is to add `#![feature(lifetime_capture_rules_2024)]` to every crate in the compiler, which seems unnecessary. If you're willing to review it, I could put up such a PR, though.

Happy to review that.

> Well, due to #116733, whether to use `use<>` over `+ 'static` (or `+ use<'a>` over `+ 'a`) in _many_ cases is now matter of taste. However, given that change was incomplete due to unsoundnesses around send bounds and uncaptured lifetime params, the fact that an opaque captures lifetimes versus doesn't capture them is still very observable (even with GATs!), so I don't see us getting around that fact any time soon, though.

I think it would be good to really outline what cases these *aren't* interchangeable. Personally, I think that in the long-term, we likely want to deprecate and/or disallow adding `+ 'a` bounds to opaque types if we move forward with `use<>`. Having *both* is definitely confusing.

body:
I'm only half-monitoring, a few comments...

Sorry @compiler-errors regarding sharing the branch before you felt it was ready, I thought the link had already been posted here.

Regarding outlives, I agree that `use<P0..Pn>` can be viewed as `+ intersection(P0...Pn)` in terms of its effects, but I would caution us a bit -- I want us to do a bit more work on modeling polonius and outlives etc in a-mir-formality, because I feel like there may be some insights derived from that on how to simplify the mental model. 

Some specific things I am thinking about are (A) the distinction between `fn foo() -> impl Bar` (which can capture lifetimes etc) and `fn foo() -> Box<dyn Bar>` (which cannot); (B) the idea of "outliving a type" which both @lcnr and I kind of independently realized was a natural thing to want in the trait solver; (C) my sense that lifetime parameters may become very rare if we opt for [place-based lifetimes](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2024/03/04/borrow-checking-without-lifetimes/); (D) the annoyance of having to desugar to `-> impl Future<Output = X>` to have an async fn that only captures some of the parameters; and (E) the sense I've found over time that if I am writing generic libraries it's better to make things parameterized over a generic *type* than a generic *lifetime* (lifetimes are useful in narrow contexts). In terms of (A), I've noticed this pattern arise sometimes: `fn process<E>(e: E) -> Box<dyn Process>`, where I get an error because the returned `dyn` captures `E`. Today I have to write `fn process<'e, E: 'e>(e: E) -> Box<dyn Process + 'e>`, which is (a) too strong for the same reasons as with `impl Trait` and (b) annoying, because `'e` isn't a natural parameter. I'd prefer to write `Box<dyn Process + use<E>>` for sure, but maybe even more than that to write `use<e>`. Anyway, I'm just thinking out loud here, but the tl;dr is that I don't want to double down on *lifetimes* per se, because I think we should be looking for how to "zoom out" and talk more about capturing places and type parameters, which are more familiar to users and often a more natural fit for what they are doing.
author: nikomatsakis

body:
> I guess, the more I think about it, the more I feel like a blog post now is "too late". I'd much rather have had more public interaction throughout the entire design process. Putting up a blog post now isn't wrong, but I get the feeling the only useful thing we could do now is have a "this is an upcoming feature and how it works" type of post - which we don't really do often, we sort of did for GATs - and monitor for feedback. I really don't expect that feedback to actually change anyone's mind here though. In large part, I think it's because really nobody has a real alternative solution. So even if the feature does turn out to be really confusing to users, we have no other option to say "is this better" and I don't expect suggestions at this point in the process to be taken seriously.

I will say @jackh726 that I agree with some parts of this -- I don't expect feedback from a blog post to change my mind. (Though you never know: the current syntax arose from an off-the-cuff suggestion by @joshtriplett that turned out to be way better than what we were thinking.) I'd definitely prefer for us to be broadcasting the 'big picture' more frequently during the design process. I've been thinking more about this since our last conversation and would like to talk again about alternatives here (but not in this thread, I think).

That said, I'd still like to see a blog post. You're not wrong that I think the broader community isn't aware of this. I want to be sure that people see the `use<>` syntax as part of a general alignment of the capture rules between async functions and other uses of impl trait -- and that they understand that most of the time they don't need to do anything at all, but now they have an explicit syntax that lets them do *precisely* the right thing when they *do* need to adjust captures. If we don't have any messaging around this, it's ripe for confusion.

I think this blog post would be great as part of a series covering the changes in the edition. It's something I've talked to @traviscross about and I'd also be happy to help drive (if that's useful...) once I'm back from vacation. I think we can base them on the great content being produced for the edition guide.

body:
I'm having mixed feelings, but it's really just... vibes I guess. Overall I've found using `addr_of!` to be "kind of ok". Obviously `&raw const a.b` is more built-in, but I'm not 100% convinced it carries its weight, and it looks "kind of funny". Though I do want to make authoring unsafe code more ergonomic in general; I don't subscribe to the philosophy that we ought to add syntactic salt just because it's unsafe, in fact I think that's quite counterproductive.

I think for me the bigger challenge is that I'm still not 100% clear on the "mental model" for validity requirements of references vs raw pointers.

body:
@rfcbot concern motivation

Sorry to do this. When I reviewed this proposal I was leaning on the heuristic of "I wasn't around for the RFC and don't need to relitigate pieces like motivation".  But the RFC was quite a long time ago, and after rereading this thread it looks like @nikomatsakis and @scottmcm both have concerns about how well motivated the solution is. I don't feel convinced either. Since Niko is on vacation it's hard to know if he would block; I'm filing this concern partly on account of that, and partly because of my own reservations.

I replied inline to some points below.. but my reading now is that this feature

* Is purely syntactic – it would be _nice_, but it doesn't fundamentally solve problems that we couldn't solve in other ways,
* Doesn't significantly improve ergonomics over `addr_of!` – in fact, it's actually longer to type, and makes it harder to invoke pointer methods,
* Is more difficult to visually parse, which _might_ lead to incorrect code given that pointers allow type casting, though I could be convinced otherwise, and
* Might actually make it harder to improve pointer types later (though as the description says, there's no proposal for this on the table)

Taken together, I'm finding myself unconvinced that we should be doing this now.

> Being macros, `addr_of`/`addr_of_mut` could in theory do arbitrary magic with the expression on which they work. The only "magic" they actually do is using the argument as a place expression rather than as a value expression.

I don't find this very motivating.. sure, macros can do anything, but if you really want to know you can look at their definition.

> Place expressions are already a subtle topic and poorly understood by many programmers; having this hidden behind a macro makes this even worse.

How would this stabilization improve matters here? It seems like we are giving people new builtin magic instead of teaching them about the subtle topic. (Which might be the right thing to do – I just don't see how this being a subtle topic counts as motivation.)

> The name `addr_of` is quite unfortunate from today's perspective, given that we have accepted provenance as a reality, which means that a pointer is _not_ just an address.

I agree that the name is unfortunate given provenance, but we could literally make a new macro with a different name if that's the main issue.

> Shouldn't we have a completely new, better raw pointer type instead? Yes we all want to see that happen

I've heard references to this but don't actually know what it's referring to.

> If we keep the `&raw $place` syntax free for this, we could use it in the future for that new type.

And also `&mut raw $place`, right?

Either way, I think having two similar syntaxes that mean different things would be confusing. I don't find it compelling as a future possibility, especially when this stabilization doesn't unblock anything.

> TBH, I'm kinda torn here because I've kinda liked the grouping that the macro provides, and I end up wanting to call methods on it often if I'm using a raw pointer -- like `addr_of!(x).cast()` -- both of which are kinda elegant with the macro.

When I first heard this my response was "sure but that's a pre-existing part of `&` syntax", but I think I should've listened more closely to what @scottmcm was saying. People who need to use raw pointers don't benefit from ergonomic mitigations like auto-ref on method receivers. If you were to mitigate this yourself by leaving parens around a bare expression like `(&raw const (*foo).thing)` rustfmt will remove them, so you have to go back and add them again if you decide to call a method. While we seem to be trying to make people's lives easier here, it seems questionable whether we are.
author: tmandry

body:
> I've heard references to this but don't actually know what it's referring to.

I don't know that there's a good resource.  But a couple of things that I think have come up before:
- there's no raw pointer type with an alignment validity invariant, which can make pointers a pessimization (slice iterators are currently lightly impacted by this, IIRC)
- see the conversations about `unsafe<'a> &'a Foo` as a type for examples of things that want a reference, not a pointer, but in a way that the lifetime is empty and thus it's not making lifetime assertions (formerly known as [`'unsafe`](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/rfc-basic-unsafe-lifetime/16873?u=scottmcm), but `&'unsafe` turned out not to work for reasons I don't remember)
- The covariant/contravariance between `*const`/`*mut`/`NonNull` isn't terribly satisfying, and needing lots of `.cast()`s in common pointer things isn't necessarily great.  It's not uncommon that you want *a* thin pointer, but don't care what its type is (see https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/103489 and https://github.com/rust-lang/libs-team/issues/362)
- (Also, fat pointers are kinda awkward in the backend, but that's not necessarily a thing needing a user-visible fix)

But maybe we don't have the correct primitive yet, and we actually want something like
```rust
struct ConstPtr<T>(Option<ptr::Opaque<1>>, T::Metadata, PhantomData<unsafe<'a> &T>);
```
for what a `*const T` really is.  (NOT a proposal, just a sketch.)

And then maybe there'd be a way that `&☃ foo.bar` would give a `Opaque<alignof(foo.bar)>` instead of a `*const`.
author: scottmcm

body:
> > Being macros, addr_of/addr_of_mut could in theory do arbitrary magic with the expression on which they work. The only "magic" they actually do is using the argument as a place expression rather than as a value expression.
> 
> I don't find this very motivating.. sure, macros can do anything, but if you really want to know you can look at their definition.

The definition uses an unstable language feature though, so you can't really look at the definition and understand what it does in the scope of stable Rust. It'd be like looking at the compiler internal implementation of an intrinsic to figure out what it does -- the result can be informative, but never authoritative.

> > Place expressions are already a subtle topic and poorly understood by many programmers; having this hidden behind a macro makes this even worse.
>
> How would this stabilization improve matters here? It seems like we are giving people new builtin magic instead of teaching them about the subtle topic. (Which might be the right thing to do – I just don't see how this being a subtle topic counts as motivation.)

It's not new magic, it's old magic. `&` and `&mut` have existed since 1.0.  By using the syntax people are already familiar with, we're cutting away a significant barrier to understanding what `addr_of!` does.

People might not understand what exactly we mean when we say "this is a place expression", but people do have an idea of what happens below `&`/`&mut`, so we can make the subtle topic a lot more approachable by connecting to existing intuition. Right now, it can easily seem like there *extra new magic* behind `addr_of!` when that is really not the case.

> I agree that the name is unfortunate given provenance, but we could literally make a new macro with a different name if that's the main issue.

When have we *ever* used a macro as the permanent and only stable way to expose a language feature? I feel like this kind of proposal needs some very serious justification.

We use macros for experimentation (`try!`, `addr_of!`), and then if the feature carries its weight we give it proper syntax.

In this case, the macro also has the big downside of entirely removing the symmetry with `&` and `&mut`, thus imposing an extra burden to understanding what this operation does.

> Either way, I think having two similar syntaxes that mean different things would be confusing. I don't find it compelling as a future possibility, especially when this stabilization doesn't unblock anything.

Having `&` and `&mut` mean different things isn't confusing, so I don't understand how this would be any more confusing in a "new pointer type world". After all, these are different *but very related*, parallel things. Parallel concepts *should* have similar syntax.

Also, indefinitely blocking proper support for our existing raw pointer types on the completely hypothetical idea for a shiny new raw pointer type *which hasn't seen any tangible progress or even serious attempts at progress in the many years since it has been first discussed* doesn't seem like a great idea to me. It is honestly quite frustrating to see attempts at small local improvements blocked on such very hypothetical ideas.

>  If you were to mitigate this yourself by leaving parens around a bare expression like (&raw const (*foo).thing) rustfmt will remove them

This is something that can be changed.

body:
> > > Being macros, addr_of/addr_of_mut could in theory do arbitrary magic with the expression on which they work. The only "magic" they actually do is using the argument as a place expression rather than as a value expression.
> > 
> > 
> > I don't find this very motivating.. sure, macros can do anything, but if you really want to know you can look at their definition.
> 
> The definition uses an unstable language feature though, so you can't really look at the definition and understand what it does in the scope of stable Rust. It'd be like looking at the compiler internal implementation of an intrinsic to figure out what it does -- the result can be informative, but never authoritative.
> 
> > > Place expressions are already a subtle topic and poorly understood by many programmers; having this hidden behind a macro makes this even worse.
> > 
> > 
> > How would this stabilization improve matters here? It seems like we are giving people new builtin magic instead of teaching them about the subtle topic. (Which might be the right thing to do – I just don't see how this being a subtle topic counts as motivation.)
> 
> It's not new magic, it's old magic. `&` and `&mut` have existed since 1.0. By using the syntax people are already familiar with, we're cutting away a significant barrier to understanding what `addr_of!` does.
> 
> People might not understand what exactly we mean when we say "this is a place expression", but people do have an idea of what happens below `&`/`&mut`, so we can make the subtle topic a lot more approachable by connecting to existing intuition. Right now, it can easily seem like there _extra new magic_ behind `addr_of!` when that is really not the case.

Thank you, this is much clearer to me in terms of motivation. Improving developers' ability to conceptualize the operational semantics of Rust does seem important, especially for the correctness and soundness of unsafe code.

I'll check that I'm not forgetting anything, but I think this resolves most or all of my concern.

> > If you were to mitigate this yourself by leaving parens around a bare expression like (&raw const (*foo).thing) rustfmt will remove them
> 
> This is something that can be changed.

Yes, I suppose it can, and maybe it should be.

While I do want to give the ergonomic question due consideration, I feel optimistic. At the very worst we could go ahead with stabilization and choose not to (soft-)deprecate `addr_of!()` until we had a solution that felt roughly as ergonomic as before. Though I'd much prefer to do it all at once, so people have clear guidance.

Separately from this proposal I'm interested in the idea of postfix `.&`, `.&mut`, `.*`, and after this, `.&raw`. That would also solve the method dispatch issue.

> When have we _ever_ used a macro as the permanent and only stable way to expose a language feature? I feel like this kind of proposal needs some very serious justification.

I wasn't actually proposing that. I was saying that if the name is the biggest issue we can address that directly, until we are ready to stabilize permanent syntax.

> Also, indefinitely blocking proper support for our existing raw pointer types on the completely hypothetical idea for a shiny new raw pointer type _which hasn't seen any tangible progress or even serious attempts at progress in the many years since it has been first discussed_ doesn't seem like a great idea to me. It is honestly quite frustrating to see attempts at small local improvements blocked on such very hypothetical ideas.

I agree that we shouldn't block on such things. My last comment is asking whether this is a real improvement on any axis of importance. Your response makes me think that it is.

To clarify where I'm coming from, I don't think we should hold out on syntax for distant hypotheticals. The general situation I am trying to avoid is using up syntax for a solution that we know has problems if we're only doing it because providing a dedicated syntax feels like the "right thing to do".

> Having `&` and `&mut` mean different things isn't confusing, so I don't understand how this would be any more confusing in a "new pointer type world". After all, these are different _but very related_, parallel things. Parallel concepts _should_ have similar syntax.

I think we might be talking about different things? Not sure. I'm saying that if in the future we had `&raw mut x` mean one type and `&mut raw x` mean another it would be highly confusing. Remembering which order to use for which case would be a real burden. We could mitigate that by deprecating the old syntax over an edition, but it's not a prospect that brings me joy.

author: RalfJung

body:
> IIRC the "future better raw pointer type" is often considered to only come in one variant, not two (`mut` and `const`).

The difficulty there is that such a type would need to be *bi*variant in order to support usage in both *co*variant and *contra*variant types, and bivariance basically means unconstrained to the rustc type system[^1]. An opaque pointer type without a pointee type is useful; one that carries a pointee type but is variance-unified with any other pointee type seems problematic.

[^1]: It's [possible to construct](https://github.com/lcnr/random-rust-snippets/issues/3) a bivariant type parameter despite unused type parameter errors, by utilizing associated type protection.

----------

My primary hesitation to stabilize the `&raw mut $place` has been the thought that we might use `&raw` as the type syntax for the improved raw pointer type, and want the expression to make that pointer type. That type might've been as simple as `*mut T` but non-null, or as involved as `MaybeDangling<unsafe<'a> &'a mut T`>, or just `ptr::WellFormed<T>`. But I don't think it's worth blocking the syntax for use today, for two main reasons: 

- An improved raw pointer type is still highly aspirational, and nowhere near being reality. 
- It's reasonably possible to make the new type decay to today's pointer type, and transition the syntax to produce the new type over an edition, if we ever find a solution to defaults affecting inference sets that we so desperately desire.

So consider this the equivalent of a checkbox from my end — this stabilization is an improvement, and it does not meaningfully prohibit desired future improvements.
author: CAD97

body:
> The difficulty there is that such a type would need to be bivariant in order to support usage in both covariant and contravariant types,

I don't see why it would need to support contravariant raw pointer types, that's an extremely rare circumstance and already not supported with our current raw pointer types.

I also don't think it should be the job of a new raw pointer type to fix the problems with our variance system; that should instead be done by allowing explicit variance annotations for type parameters of a generic type. The raw pointer type can then be invariant for a maximally safe default, and types that want covariance (or contravariance) can opt-in to that explicitly.

But anyway this is getting rather off-topic for this thread.

@rfcbot resolve motivation

This stabilization has a big impact in terms of syntax, but it makes it easier for Rust users to learn how to use unsafe. The negative ergonomic impacts of moving from `addr_of!` can be mitigated in the ways I mention below.

> I don't know when exactly rustfmt currently auto-removes parentheses, and in which cases you'd prefer that to not happen. Are you thinking of `let ptr = (&raw const <expr>);`?

Yes. Actually I misremembered; it's the rustc `unnecessary_parentheses` lint, not rustfmt that enforces this.

Maybe if we just relax that lint in the case where it's around `&raw {const|mut}` expressions, that's good enough. I would be comfortable telling people to use this instead of `addr_of!` then. It's not as good as `.&raw` but that can come later.

> * Is more difficult to visually parse, which _might_ lead to incorrect code given that pointers allow type casting, though I could be convinced otherwise, and

Following up on my own point, I can't think of examples where this would lead to bugs.

body:

Just sanity checks because I'm paranoid due to reviewing run-make tests. I don't think you missed any tests.

Feel free to r=me and TC after the try-jobs come back green.

body: I don't think this PR is particularly likely to cause strange problems that wouldn't be caught by PR CI, and even then if we don't have any concrete suspicion generally I think we just `r+` these and let bors catch those cases. The queue is also rather empty right now so it's not like we'd be wasting precious bors slots.
author: RalfJung

body: Fair enough. Unfortunately I can't cancel the try-jobs now, and we can't r+ immediately either when a try build is on-going or else bors can (or will) push this to master without any testing.

body:
> Not sure in which order we usually do this -- should the implementation PR close the tracking issue, or should the reference PR do that?

For tracking purposes, I think it's most logical if whichever merges last closes the tracking issue. But that's probably up to T-lang, I don't really mind.
